property_summary: Only the owner can withdraw the contract balance: after a non-owner sends ether to C, only the original owner can reduce address(c).balance to zero via withdrawAll.
If a caller who is not the contract owner calls withdrawAll, the call must revert (i.e., non-owners cannot successfully call withdrawAll).
Calls to withdrawAll revert for callers that are not the contract owner.
If the InvMutTest contract (address(this)) calls withdrawAll on c, the call must revert (i.e., non-owner callers cannot successfully call withdrawAll).

For any nonzero contract balance, calling withdrawAll by the owner empties the contract (address(c).balance becomes 0) in the reference; the mutant that subtracts 1 wei leaves the contract with 1 wei for some fuzzed balance values and thus violates this rule.

For any initial contract balance funded by the owner, calling withdrawAll by the owner reduces the contract balance to 0 (reference); the mutant that withdraws balance-1 leaves 1 wei behind for balances >=1, violating this rule.

For any non-owner-funded balance X >= 1 where the owner calls withdrawAll, the correct contract transfers the full contract balance so address(c).balance becomes 0; the mutant that withdraws balance-1 leaves 1 wei behind, so address(c).balance != 0 for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and for any initial contract balance B that is exactly funded by the owner, calling withdrawAll results in the contract balance becoming 0 (the buggy mutant that subtracts 1 wei will leave 1 wei when B >= 1).

For any amount A >= 1 funded into the contract by anypaying address (not necessarily the owner), if the owner calls withdrawAll() the reference contract forwards the entire contract balance to the owner (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant subtracting 1 wei from the balance causes the contract to sometimes retain 1 wei, so address(c).balance != 0 for some fuzzed A and payer.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any recipient address used as tx.origin, calling withdraw(uint) transfers the withdrawn amount to msg.sender (the owner) so that address(c).balance decreases by that amount; the mutant sends funds to tx.origin instead which can make address(c).balance unchanged when tx.origin != msg.sender or send funds to a different address, violating this property for some fuzzed inputs.

After owner calls withdraw(value), the contract's balance always decreases by that value (reference C sends withdrawn funds to msg.sender/owner), but the mutant sending to tx.origin can leave the contract balance unchanged for inputs where tx.origin != msg.sender (e.g., when owner is a contract), so the rule is violated for some inputs.

For any caller (owner) and any target callee, when the owner calls withdraw(x) the contract's balance decreases by x (the reference sends to msg.sender) — the mutant sending to tx.origin can keep the contract balance unchanged when the owner is a contract (tx.origin != msg.sender), violating this rule for some inputs.

For every caller who is the owner (msg.sender == owner) the reference contract always transfers withdrawn ETH to msg.sender so address(c).balance decreases by the withdrawn amount; the mutant sends to tx.origin instead, which can keep address(c).balance unchanged when the owner is a contract (msg.sender != tx.origin), so the mutant violates this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For any address owner that calls withdraw(amount) the reference contract always sends the withdrawn ETH to msg.sender (so msg.sender receives the funds), whereas the mutant sends to tx.origin which will differ when the owner is a contract calling via an intermediate EOA, breaking the property for such inputs.

For all callers and amounts, only the externally-owned owner address (msg.sender == owner) can successfully withdraw funds from the contract; the mutant which also allows msg.sender == address(this) permits the contract itself to call withdraw and thus can change post-withdraw state for some inputs (e.g. when the contract is the msg.sender), violating the rule.

For every caller and value, only an externally-owned address equal to owner or external calls originating from other EOAs should ever allow a successful withdraw initiated by that caller; specifically, the correct contract never allows a withdraw call where msg.sender == address(c) (the contract calling itself) to succeed, while the mutant does — so the property is: any successful withdraw must have msg.sender == owner and cannot have msg.sender == address(c).

For every caller and amount, any successful withdraw call must have msg.sender == owner (i.e., the contract itself must never be able to be the msg.sender when withdraw succeeds); the mutant relaxing onlyOwner to allow msg.sender==address(this) lets a withdraw succeed with msg.sender==address(c) for some inputs, violating this rule.

For all inputs and callers, any successful withdraw() call on the correct contract only succeeds when msg.sender == owner (i.e. withdraw cannot be successfully invoked by the contract itself); the mutant relaxes onlyOwner to allow msg.sender == address(this), so there exist inputs where withdraw succeeds with msg.sender == address(c), violating the rule.

In the reference C, any successful call to withdraw must originate from the owner externally (msg.sender == owner); the mutant additionally allows withdraw when msg.sender == address(this), so there exist inputs where a withdraw call initiated by the contract itself succeeds and thus breaks the rule.

For any nonzero amount sent to the contract beforehand, calling withdraw(amount) by the owner reduces the contract balance by exactly that amount (i.e. address(c).balance decreases by _value); the mutant that always transfers 0 breaks this rule for some amount > 0.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(x) after the contract has held at least x wei, the contract's balance decreases by x (the correct C transfers _value to owner); the mutant that transfers 0 breaks this because the balance does not decrease for some x>0.

For any nonzero amount x and when the contract holds at least x wei, calling withdraw(x) by the owner results in the owner's received balance increasing by x (i.e., the owner actually gets the funds); the mutant that always transfers 0 violates this because the owner's balance does not increase for some x>0.

For any owner address and any deposit amount x that the contract holds, calling withdraw(x) always transfers exactly x wei to the owner (so address(c).balance decreases by x and owner balance increases by x); the mutant that always transfers 0 breaks this rule for some x>0.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(amount) call, the contract's depositsCount (which increments only on fallback payable calls) is unchanged by withdraw; the bug changes withdraw to transfer 0 but does not change depositsCount — however the observable difference is that withdraw should forward the requested amount to the owner (via transfer) which will revert if owner is a contract whose receive() reverts on 0 vs non-zero value; specifically, when owner is a contract whose payable fallback reverts on zero-value transfers but accepts non-zero transfers, the correct contract's withdraw(amount>0) succeeds while the mutant's withdraw(>0) sends 0 and thus triggers the owner's revert behavior — therefore the property: for any positive amount and an owner contract that reverts on zero-value transfers but accepts non-zero, withdraw(amount) must succeed (return without revert) on the reference but the mutant call will revert for some amount.
After sending some funds via sendMoney, the target address's balance increases by exactly the provided _value (so address(c).balance decreases by that same _value).

For any caller-supplied target and amount, when the owner calls sendMoney with value v the contract's balance decreases by exactly v (reference) — the mutant that always sends 0 wei will not decrease the contract balance for some v>0.
